div.head: III Atr 13
div.ab: ⁊ gif man hwilcne man téo, þæt he þone man féde, þe ures hlafordes grið tóbrocen habbe, ladige hine mid þrinna XII; ⁊ se geréfa namige þa lade.
Et si aliquis accusetur, quod eum pauerit, qui pacem domini nostri fregerit, ladiet se mid þrinna XII (id est cum ter XII, qui faciunt triginta sex); et prepositus nominet ipsam ladam.
⁊ gif man hwilcne man téo, þæt he þone man féde þe ures hlafordes grið tóbrocen habbe, ladige hine mid þrinna XII, ⁊ se geréfa namige þa lade.

Und wenn irgend welcher Mann beschuldigt wird, dass er einen Menschen, der den von unserem Herrn [König verliehenen] Sonderschutz gebrochen hat, beköstige, so reinige er sich mit drei[mal] 12; und der [Königs]vogt ernenne diese [Eideshelfer der] Reinigung.

And if any man is accused of feeding a person who has broken the special protection [granted] by our lord [the king], let him clear himself with three [times] 12; and let the [king's] reeve name those [oath-helpers for the] clearing.
And if anyone is accused of furnishing with food a man who has broken our lord's peace, he shall clear himself with three times twelve compurgators who shall be nominated by the reeve.
And if anyone is charged with feeding a man who has broken our lord’s peace, he is to clear himself with three twelves; and the reeve is to nominate the compurgators.

note.seg: Nur Bruch des Handfriedens, nicht jedes Königsfriedens, macht friedlos (s. o. 1), und nur Begünstigung (s. d. 8. b) des Friedlosen ist mit Friedlosigkeit strafbar
Only breach of the hand-given peace, not of every king's peace, makes a man an outlaw (see above 1), and only harbouring (see that word 8. b) of the outlaw is punishable with outlawry

Das Nord. Wort war dem Q anfangs unverständlich. Schon Price zitierte aus Stadtrecht von Lund threnne tylter: [Eideshilfe von] drei Zwölfern. Vgl. Toller 605b vorl. Z.
The Norse word was at first unintelligible to Q. Price already quoted from the town law of Lund threnne tylter: [oath-help of] three twelves. Cf. Toller 605b, last l. but one

A Scandinavian mode of expressing number, cf. þrennar tylftir (Njalssaga, Ch. 144). The right of refuting charges by means of 36 compurgators is found in London and elsewhere from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries (see Bateson, Borough Customs, i. pp. 37–44; Gross, Modes of Trial in Mediaeval Boroughs, H.L.R. 15. p. 695 ff.).
